summary: Zephaniah 3 first confronts Jerusalem as a rebellious city whose leaders, prophets, and priests have failed while Yahweh remains righteous within her. The chapter then moves from judgment on gathered nations to purified worship, a humble remnant, and a closing promise that Jerusalem will rejoice because Yahweh is among the people and will gather the shamed and displaced.
whyItMatters: This chapter brings the book's warnings back to Jerusalem before ending with its broadest vision of restoration. The final hope does not erase the earlier judgment; it imagines changed speech, removed arrogance, refuge, joy, and gathering.

context.author: The heading of the book names Zephaniah son of Cushi and traces his ancestry to Hezekiah; a connection to King Hezekiah is possible but unproved.
context.audience: Judah and Jerusalem are central, while the book also addresses surrounding peoples and ends with a horizon that includes the nations' worship.
context.date: The heading places the message in Josiah's reign, conventionally 640-609 BCE; the final formation of the book is a separate question debated by scholars.
context.setting: Judah and Jerusalem stand within the world of Assyrian power, with the book moving between local accusation, surrounding nations, and a restored community.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic poetry with accusation, divine speech, warning, command, and restoration promise.

outline.heading: Jerusalem accused
outline.note: The city is called rebellious, polluted, and oppressive, and its refusal is described in four short statements.

outline.heading: Leaders indicted, God contrasted
outline.note: Princes, judges, prophets, and priests are portrayed as predatory or corrupt, while Yahweh is righteous within the city.

outline.heading: Warnings ignored
outline.note: Destroyed nations should have taught fear and correction, but the city corrupts its actions instead.

outline.heading: Nations gathered, worship purified
outline.note: Yahweh announces judgment on the nations, then describes purified lips and worshipers bringing an offering.

outline.heading: A humble remnant
outline.note: Arrogance is removed, an afflicted and poor people take refuge, and the remnant is described as truthful and unafraid.

outline.heading: Jerusalem told to rejoice
outline.note: Zion and Jerusalem are summoned to joy because judgments and enemies are removed and Yahweh is among them.

outline.heading: From festival grief to rescue and honor
outline.note: The difficult verse 18 speaks of removing festival mourners in WEB; verses 19-20 promise rescue for the lame, gathering of the driven away, and restored honor and fortunes.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, within her, is righteous. He will do no wrong. Every morning he brings his justice to light. He doesn’t fail, but the unjust know no shame.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the contrast between Jerusalem's failed leaders and Yahweh's justice within the city.

keyVerses.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on Yahweh’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
keyVerses.why: The chapter turns from judgment toward changed speech and shared worship among the peoples.

keyVerses.text: But I will leave among you an afflicted and poor people, and they will take refuge in Yahweh’s name.
keyVerses.why: This identifies the restored community not by power or pride but by vulnerability and refuge.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.
keyVerses.why: Yahweh's presence, rescue, love, and joy over Jerusalem anchor the closing hope. The love clause differs across translations: WEB has calm, KJV rest, Douay-Rheims silence, and Brenton refreshment. The Hebrew text uses a verb of silence, so the precise sense should not be treated as undisputed.

questions.question: Who is the city in the opening verses?
questions.answer: The city is unnamed in verse 1 but is understood as Jerusalem, returning the accusation to Judah after the judgment on Nineveh in chapter 2. Verse 14 explicitly addresses daughter of Zion, Israel, and daughter of Jerusalem. The chapter moves from Jerusalem confronted to Jerusalem restored.

questions.question: What does the city refuse to do?
questions.answer: Verse 2 piles up four refusals: the city does not obey, receive correction, trust in Yahweh, or draw near to God. The point is not one isolated mistake but a pattern of resistance across listening, learning, trust, and worship.

questions.question: Why compare princes and judges to lions and wolves?
questions.answer: The images portray public officials as dangerous to the people they should protect. Princes are called roaring lions, and judges are evening wolves that leave nothing until the next day, so the focus is predatory leadership within the city.

questions.question: What have the prophets and priests done wrong?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says the prophets are arrogant and treacherous. It says the priests have profaned the sanctuary and done violence to the law, so the chapter accuses religious leaders as well as political leaders.

questions.question: How can Yahweh be 'within her' when the city is corrupt?
questions.answer: The chapter holds those claims side by side. Corrupt leaders are within the city in verses 3-4, but verse 5 says Yahweh is also within her and is righteous. Later the same theme returns positively when Yahweh is among the restored people.

questions.question: What is difficult about verse 8?
questions.answer: Verse 8 commands waiting for Yahweh until the day he rises up and gathers nations for judgment. Where WEB and KJV say he rises up to the prey, Brenton has a witness and Douay-Rheims speaks of resurrection. These are real translation differences; the last wording alone does not establish a prediction of Christ's resurrection. Across the chapter, judgment on gathered kingdoms precedes the promise of purified worship in verse 9.

questions.question: Does verse 9 mean everyone will speak one new language?
questions.answer: The verse says Yahweh will purify the lips of the peoples so they may call on his name and serve shoulder to shoulder. The imagery is about changed speech and shared service. It does not explicitly describe the invention of one new human language.

questions.question: Who are the 'afflicted and poor people'?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says Yahweh will leave an afflicted and poor people who take refuge in his name. Their description includes actual hardship as well as humble reliance on God: verse 19 also names people who are lame and those driven away. The restored community includes socially vulnerable and displaced people.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end with singing and gathering?
questions.answer: Verses 14-17 summon Jerusalem to rejoice because judgment and fear are removed and Yahweh is among the people. Verse 18 begins divine first-person speech, but its wording is difficult: WEB removes those grieving about the appointed feasts, while other translations speak of gathering. The clear rescue and gathering promises come in verses 19-20, where Yahweh saves the lame, gathers the driven away, and restores their honor and fortunes. The ending presents a public reversal of shame without making every detail of verse 18 certain.

glossary.def: A word that introduces grief, warning, or accusation; here it opens the confrontation with the rebellious city.
A description of the city in verse 1, paired with rebellion and oppression rather than explained as physical dirt.
The holy place connected with worship; verse 4 says the priests have profaned it.
The remaining people of Israel described in verse 13 after arrogance has been removed and refuge has been promised.
Named gatherings or festival times mentioned in verse 18, where the line is difficult but the concern is tied to grief, burden, and reproach.
